The admin account is explicitly described as a single account per registry with full permissions, designed for one user and not for sharing, and its two passwords exist to allow rotation without downtime, not to make sharing acceptable. Repository-scoped tokens are the nearest wrong option and would improve attribution, but Microsoft states that token-based repository permissions do not support Microsoft Entra RBAC role assignments, which is exactly the governance the auditor wants.

wf-33-06.why: Microsoft calls this out directly: an AKS cluster does not have a fixed outbound address by default, so a registry restricted to specific IPs may reject it, and the fix is to control egress traffic for the Standard load balancer or to move to Private Link, where IP rules do not apply at all. Disabling public network access is the nearest wrong option and sounds like more security, but it overrides all firewall configuration and would break the build servers too; and it would also cut virtual network access if the registry uses a service endpoint. A registry supports up to 200 IP access rules, so the limit answer is simply wrong.

wf-33-07.why: Functions access keys come in scopes: a function key authorizes only one function endpoint, a host key authorizes every function endpoint in the app, and the master key additionally grants administrative access to the runtime REST APIs. Handing over the host key shown on App keys is the nearest wrong option, and it is exactly the trap here, because that page is where the engineer was already looking, but it would grant the partner every other endpoint in the app. System keys are real but are created only by specific extensions for internal callers such as an Event Grid subscription, and their values cannot be set by you.

wf-33-08.why: For Consumption workflows, a request-based trigger endpoint accepts exactly one inbound authorization scheme, Microsoft Entra OAuth 2.0 or SAS. Enabling one does not switch the other off, and using both at once produces an error because the service cannot choose, so the correct completion is to disable SAS and restrict authorization to Entra. The nearest wrong option is leaving SAS as a fallback: there is no documented precedence between the two schemes, and leaving the SAS keys live keeps the callable-URL secret in circulation, which was the compliance objection. Standard workflows behave differently and may combine other authentication types with SAS still enabled.

wf-33-09.why: Service tag rules filter inbound traffic to well-known Azure service ranges, and App Service supports HTTP header filtering on any rule, with X-Azure-FDID documented for identifying a specific reverse proxy instance. Combining them is the named use case, because the service tag alone would still admit any customer's Front Door profile. The nearest wrong option is an IP-based rule: Microsoft states that these rules cover virtual network ranges only when the app runs in an App Service Environment, and Front Door does not present a stable customer-owned range in the multitenant service. Enabling authentication protects the application session but does not stop the origin from being reached around the WAF.

wf-33-10.why: Container Apps documents managed identity image pull as the pattern that avoids registry administrative credentials and gives fine-grained access through the AcrPull role, and its secrets guidance is to avoid holding production secrets in Container Apps directly and to use Key Vault references instead. The nearest wrong option is the token store, which is a genuine Container Apps feature but stores end-user authentication tokens in Blob Storage for the built-in auth flow; it has nothing to do with registry or database credentials. Moving secrets into plain environment variables makes the exposure worse, not better.

wf-33-11.why: Anomaly scoring blocks at a total of 5, so a Warning at 3 plus an Error at 4 crosses the threshold even though neither would alone; the surgical containment is an exclusion narrowed to the offending request attribute and rule, which Microsoft explicitly recommends over broader exclusions. The nearest wrong option is the custom rule with an Allow action, which would work and is tempting under pressure, but an Allow short-circuits all lower-priority evaluation so the entire notes endpoint stops being inspected for SQL injection and cross-site scripting. Switching the policy to detection mode disarms the WAF for every site behind it, and the anomaly threshold of 5 is not a customer-tunable dial.

wf-33-12.why: Binary drift is the sensor-based capability aimed exactly at processes that were not in the image, and it has both a detection mode and a blocking mode where you define drift policies specifying the conditions under which processes are blocked. That is the only option that stops the running process. The nearest wrong option is the network policy: cutting egress is a reasonable parallel action and would degrade the miner's usefulness, but the process keeps consuming the nodes and the pod stays compromised. The allowed-images recommendation is admission control, so its Deny effect governs the next scheduling decision rather than the container already running.

wf-33-13.why: Microsoft's OWASP API guidance names rate limiting as the mitigation that blunts brute-force and credential-stuffing pressure, and recommends stricter limits on sensitive endpoints such as sign-in and password reset; rate-limit-by-key throttles per key over a sliding window of up to 300 seconds and returns 429 to callers who exceed it. The nearest wrong option is quota-by-key, which is a real and related policy but is designed for long time frames and total consumption budgeting, so it neither reacts within the hour nor protects the backend from a burst. An allow-action ip-filter would lock out every legitimate retail customer, and validate-jwt cannot help on an endpoint whose whole job is to issue credentials to anonymous callers.

wf-33-14.why: The master key is a host key with administrative reach over the runtime REST APIs under the admin path, so renewal is the only thing that revokes the attacker's access, and Functions supports disabling administrative endpoints through the functionsRuntimeAdminIsolationEnabled site property, which removes the attack surface rather than just the credential. The nearest wrong option is rotating function keys: precedence between function and host keys only decides which key is used when two share a name, and it does nothing to invalidate _master. Blocking one address defers the rotation while the key is still valid and published, and changing the secret storage location moves where keys live without revoking their values.

wf-33-15.why: Microsoft's API Management guidance is explicit that for defence in depth a WAF should be deployed upstream of the instance, using Application Gateway or Front Door, and its resource-consumption recommendations point at bot protection with the Microsoft bot manager rule set in front of the gateway for layer 7 pressure. The nearest wrong option is private endpoints, which is genuinely recommended for hiding internal API endpoints from the internet, but these are public consumer APIs that must stay reachable, so Private Link solves a different problem. Client certificates strengthen caller identity yet do nothing about volumetric floods, and a second region adds capacity rather than inspection.

wf-33-16.why: AKS registry-security guidance names image signing and verification with the Notary Project as the way to prove provenance, and Kubernetes data plane hardening includes a recommendation that container images be deployed from trusted registries only, which is one of the recommendations requiring you to configure the registry list as a policy parameter and can be moved from audit to Deny. Docker Content Trust is the nearest wrong option precisely because it is already on: Microsoft has closed it to new registries as of May 2026 and is removing it entirely in March 2028, with a documented transition to Notary. The Defender vulnerability findings artifact is signed by Microsoft for the integrity of the findings themselves and is not an image provenance control, and image cleaner removes unused vulnerable images rather than enforcing origin.

wf-41-01.why: Risk prioritization, attack path analysis and governance are capabilities of the paid Defender CSPM plan; without it those columns render blurred in the recommendations experience. Defender for Servers Plan 2 is the nearest miss because it does bring agentless machine scanning and vulnerability findings, but it is a workload protection plan and does not unlock risk-based ranking of recommendations. MCSB is already applied by default the moment Defender for Cloud is enabled, so assigning it changes nothing.

wf-41-02.why: Cloud security explorer lets you run your own path-finding queries over the cloud security graph, correlating exposure, identity permissions, and data sensitivity in one question. Attack path analysis is the closest wrong answer: it surfaces only the exploitable paths the proprietary algorithm has already computed and ranked, so it cannot be steered at an arbitrary ad hoc correlation. Resource Graph reaches asset and assessment records but not the graph relationships between identity, exposure and data.

wf-41-03.why: Standards beyond the defaults can only be added once at least one paid plan is on for the scope, and they are assigned from Manage compliance policies against the account or management account; Microsoft advises picking the highest applicable scope so nested resources aggregate. Assigning the Azure Policy initiative is the tempting near miss, because Azure standards do ride on policy initiatives, but that path assesses Azure resources and will not evaluate AWS resources reached through the connector. Compliance Manager consumes the resulting data rather than producing it.

wf-41-04.why: Standards mix automated and manual assessments; manual ones are cleared by selecting the assessment, choosing the subscriptions, selecting Attest and attaching evidence, which is exactly the audit artefact wanted. An exemption is the plausible wrong turn, since it also removes a red mark, but it records that a requirement is being skipped rather than demonstrating it is met. Waiting achieves nothing because a control with no automatable signal never resolves itself, and disable rules belong to vulnerability findings, not compliance controls.

wf-41-05.why: Plan 1 is the entry-level tier built around the Defender for Endpoint integration and it is the only Servers plan that can be enabled at resource level, which the Security Center granular pricing policy definitions do by tag. Plan 2 at resource level is the trap: Plan 2 can only be disabled per resource, never enabled per resource, so that assignment cannot exist. Exclusion tags on agentless scanning only skip scanning, they do not stop the subscription from being billed or protected, and CSPM alone brings posture scanning rather than endpoint detection and response.

wf-41-06.why: Microsoft recommends policy-based enablement precisely for this case: it applies one consistent configuration across every current and future storage account inside the scope, including whole management groups. Toggling each subscription in the portal is the near miss, because it does protect accounts that exist now, but nothing carries the setting to subscriptions or accounts created later. Workflow automation reacts after the fact and Defender CSPM gives posture and data discovery, not the storage threat detection and malware scanning of the workload plan.

wf-41-07.why: Management account onboarding auto-provisions connectors for discovered member accounts and for accounts created later, and when onboarding a management account the CloudFormation template must be run as a Stack and as a StackSet, with AWS Organizations trusted access enabled. Using the delegated administrator account is the seductive wrong answer because it matches normal AWS practice, but Defender for Cloud explicitly does not support delegated administrator accounts for this. An account already wired to Microsoft Sentinel needs the separate documented procedure rather than inheriting anything.

wf-41-08.why: Defender for Cloud reaches Google Cloud through federated trust, using a workload identity pool plus impersonation of purpose-built service accounts, so no long-lived secret is stored anywhere; the script provisions the pool, per-plan providers, service accounts and project-level bindings, and APIs such as the IAM, STS, resource manager, IAM credentials and compute services must be enabled, on the management project for organization onboarding. The JSON key answer is the trap because that is how many third-party tools still work. Azure Arc matters for Defender for Servers coverage of GCP virtual machines, but it is not the connector authentication mechanism.

wf-41-09.why: Agentless machine scanning skips virtual machines whose disks use unsupported types, and ultra disk is on that unsupported list along with premium v2 and AKS ephemeral OS disks, so the only route to findings for those hosts is agent-based scanning through the Defender for Endpoint sensor, which Plan 1 and Plan 2 both provide. Exclusion tags are the plausible first guess, and worth checking, but they would not correlate so neatly with a single storage choice. Scan frequency is not adjustable: agentless scanning runs on a fixed daily cycle.

wf-41-10.why: Monitor Only is defined for assets that are relevant to your attack surface but are neither directly controlled by you nor a technical dependency, and Microsoft gives independent franchisees and related companies as the example, which is exactly this relationship. Dependency is the closest wrong option and is reserved for third-party infrastructure that directly supports the operation of your own assets, such as a hosting provider carrying your web content. Requires Investigation is a triage state pending a decision, not the decision itself.

wf-41-11.why: Attack paths start at an external entry point and run through lateral movement to a critical target, and the remediation tab separates recommendations that mitigate the path from additional ones that only reduce exploitation risk, so removing the external reachability severs the chain immediately even before patching completes. Chasing the highest scoring control is the plausible misfire because it optimises secure score rather than this live chain, and secure score weighting is unrelated to the path in front of you. An exemption hides the finding while the route stays open, and note the path itself can take up to 24 hours to disappear after real remediation.

wf-41-12.why: Malware scanning is capped per storage account per month for cost control, defaulting to ten thousand gigabytes, and the plan supports overriding subscription-level settings for a specific account, which is exactly the lever that restores scanning without touching every other account. Enabling sensitive data threat detection is the nearest wrong answer because it is a genuine Defender for Storage feature and sounds like more inspection, but it detects exposure of sensitive data rather than scanning uploads for malware. Agentless machine scanning covers virtual machine disks, not blob uploads.

wf-41-13.why: Enabling a new Defender plan or changing plan configuration such as regions is exactly the documented trigger for refreshing the CloudFormation template, and the fix is to generate the current template and update the existing stack, keeping the stack parameters and acknowledging the IAM changes. Deleting and recreating the connector is the panic option: it discards history and configuration for a problem that a stack update solves. There is no long-lived access key to rotate, because authentication is federated with short-lived credentials, and the gcloud script belongs to GCP onboarding.

wf-41-14.why: Discovery works by recursing outward from known assets through Whois records, DNS records, shared certificates and address block or ASN relationships, so an already indexed compromised host is itself a lead into the rest of the unmanaged estate that was built alongside it. Adding an exclusion is the actively harmful option: exclusions keep entities out of inventory, which is the opposite of what an investigation needs. Seeding a one-off group with a single host narrows the aperture, and waiting for the weekly cadence spends the hour you do not have.

wf-41-15.why: Disabled findings are invisible and do not affect secure score, which is precisely how a CVE hides for months; Microsoft is deprecating disable rules as part of the move to individual recommendations and directs teams to exemptions, which carry the exception explicitly. Raising the minimum severity is the tempting half-measure because it narrows the blast radius, but it leaves the same silent suppression mechanism in place. Exclusion tags stop machines being scanned at all, which is a wider hole, not a narrower one.

wf-41-16.why: Governance is the Defender CSPM capability built for exactly this failure mode: it drives remediation at scale by assigning owners and due dates and tracking whether the estate is converging on the security policy. Enforce and deny is the strong nearby answer and belongs in the hardening plan, but it prevents future noncompliant resources rather than closing the twelve findings already sitting there with no owner. Workflow automation and continuous export move information around; neither creates accountability or a deadline.

wf-42-01.why: The Defender portal supports one primary workspace plus any number of secondary ones, and the Defender XDR connector attaches to the primary workspace alone. Incident creation and alert correlation stay separated per workspace. The nearest wrong answer is enabling a second XDR connector: any standalone Microsoft connectors on secondary workspaces are deliberately disconnected at onboarding precisely to stop tenant-based alerts being counted twice, so that path is blocked by design rather than merely inadvisable.

wf-42-02.why: Installing, updating, and removing content hub items requires Microsoft Sentinel Contributor at resource group level, and that role also carries the create and edit rights for analytics rules she needs. The closest wrong choice is Playbook Operator: it only lets someone list, view, and manually run playbooks, and it grants nothing at all in the content hub. Responder alone stops at managing incidents.

wf-42-03.why: Vendor solutions that ride on the unified Azure Monitor Agent connectors for CEF, Syslog, or custom logs declare dependencies, and Install with dependencies pulls in the solution that actually carries the connector. The tempting wrong answer is the pre-created table: that requirement belongs to Custom Logs via AMA, where you build the table ending in _CL yourself, not to CEF collection, which lands in the built-in CommonSecurityLog table.

wf-42-04.why: A policy assignment governs resources created from that point on; a remediation task is what reaches back and applies the diagnostic setting to resources that already exist. The nearest wrong option, clearing the parameter filter, is a real step in the same wizard but only exposes the workspace and log-type parameters, and does nothing about existing scope. Retention changes never backfill data that was never ingested.

wf-42-05.why: When the source cannot be moved to a different facility, the documented remedy is a KQL transformation on the DCR that filters CEF messages out of the syslog stream, checking both the process name and the message body because some vendors do not honour the RFC header format. The closest wrong answer, a second forwarder, splits the machines but not the facility, so the same facility still feeds both streams and the duplication survives. Repointing CEF at Microsoft-Syslog would simply destroy the CommonSecurityLog parsing.

wf-42-06.why: Minimal is defined as the small breach-indicative set: it keeps successful and failed logons and process creation while deliberately omitting sign-out, which is high volume and of little detection value. The nearest wrong choice is Common, which exists to keep a full audit trail including 4634, so it holds precisely the records the lead agreed to give up. Custom XPath would reach the same place but is unnecessary work when a prebuilt set already expresses the requirement.

wf-42-07.why: Windows Event Forwarding concentrates events on a collector, so the agent belongs on the collector, and the connector prerequisite is exactly that: WEC enabled and running with the agent on that machine. Installing the agent on every source, the closest wrong option, defeats the whole reason the estate was designed this way and is not what the connector expects. The forwarder script and the _CL table belong to Linux syslog and text-file collection respectively.

wf-42-08.why: The destination table must carry the _CL suffix and just two columns, a datetime and the whole log line. The line column is called RawData when collection happens on the machine hosting the application, and Message when a log forwarder sits in between, which is the case here and is why the paired transformation renames the field. The RawData variant is the near miss: correct shape, wrong field name for this topology. The _SRCH suffix belongs to tables produced by search jobs.

wf-42-09.why: Automation rules run playbooks under a dedicated Sentinel service account, not under the author, and that account must be granted rights on the resource group where the playbook lives; the Manage playbook permissions link does this and asks for Owner on the group. The nearest wrong answer, Playbook Operator for the engineer, only enables that person to run a playbook by hand, which does nothing for unattended execution. Trigger type is irrelevant here; both trigger families can call playbooks of the matching type.

wf-42-10.why: Analytics retention is the expensive hot window and 90 days covers the hunters, while total retention carries the same table onward in the lake for up to twelve years at low cost, which satisfies the regulator. Moving the whole table to the Data Lake tier is the tempting alternative but it stops real-time analytics rules, alerting, and hunting on that table entirely, so the three-month working window disappears. Leaving 180 days hot simply pays twice as much for a window nobody uses.

wf-42-11.why: Events not selected by the rule were never sent, so the only way forward is to widen what the agent collects, and editing the rule in place applies to every associated machine without a second association to manage. Standing up a second rule with All events is the close alternative: it works, but it floods the workspace with the full unfiltered Security and AppLocker channels mid-incident and leaves a rule to unpick afterwards. Retention and search jobs only reach data that was already ingested, and these records never were.

wf-42-12.why: Non-playbook actions such as tagging and assignment run natively, so a rule that performs those but silently skips the playbook points squarely at the Sentinel service account lacking rights on the playbook resource group. Reordering, the nearest wrong answer, changes which rule runs first but never grants the missing permission, so the action would still be skipped. Both Logic Apps plans are supported from automation rules, and switching to the alert trigger would abandon the incident-shaped conditions the rule depends on.

wf-42-13.why: Data Lake tier data is deliberately outside real-time features, so alerting, analytics rules, and hunting stop the moment a table is moved there, and the tier must be changed back for detections to resume on incoming data. The lake is still readable through KQL jobs and notebooks, which is how the overnight window gets examined without waiting. Rewriting the rules against the lake, the nearest wrong answer, is not possible in the way it sounds because scheduled analytics rules are among the features the lake tier does not support.

wf-42-14.why: Defender XDR administrative actions, including creating or editing custom detection rules and creating or removing indicators of compromise, are audited automatically into Microsoft Purview Audit and are searchable from the Audit page in the Defender portal by activity, date, and user. CloudAuditEvents is the closest-looking distractor but it holds cloud platform control-plane records surfaced by Defender for Cloud, not portal administration of Defender XDR, and it returns nothing at all if Defender for Cloud is not in play. SentinelHealth reports connector health, not who changed what.

wf-42-15.why: SentinelHealth only exists once health monitoring is enabled, and Microsoft's guidance is to alert on health drift with Azure Monitor alert rules rather than analytics rules, which is what turns a silent feed into a page. Table insights is the seductive wrong answer because its Last data received and fluctuation cards do surface exactly this symptom, but the documentation is explicit that it is a visualization surface, not an alerting one, and tables below a megabyte a day are not even evaluated. Automation rules react to incidents, so they cannot fire on the absence of data.

wf-42-16.why: Syslog and CEF records are not Azure resources, so they inherit the resource ID of the forwarding VM, which means one shared forwarder makes every team's events indistinguishable for access purposes; separate forwarders per team, each with a resource ID, is the documented way to make resource-context RBAC work here. Sentinel Reader is the closest wrong answer and fails the requirement in the opposite direction, since it opens the whole workspace and the Sentinel experience rather than a slice of it. A second workspace would solve the permission problem but is heavy, and cross-workspace querying would reintroduce the exposure.

wf-43-01.why: A non-E5 and non-E7 tenant follows manual onboarding: it names a workspace, then provisions SCU capacity against an Azure subscription and resource group, which needs Azure Contributor or Owner on that resource group and Security Administrator or higher in the tenant. The nearest wrong answer is the E5 upgrade, which is a real path to inclusion capacity but not a prerequisite, since manual provisioning exists precisely so lower-licensed tenants can buy SCUs starting at one unit.

wf-43-02.why: Provisioned capacity grants the full unit count each clock hour, for example 02:00 to 03:00, and anything unused simply lapses when that hour ends. The rolling-window option is the trap because it sounds like the same idea, but a rolling sixty minutes from session start would let a heavy user shift capacity around, and Microsoft explicitly documents fixed hour blocks rather than rolling ones.

wf-43-03.why: Provisioned capacity bills in whole hourly blocks with a one hour minimum, so two separate provisions inside the 09:00 hour are two billed units, and the documented advice is to change unit counts at the top of the hour. The overage answer is the closest miss: overage really is consumption-based and billed to one decimal place, but it does not exempt anything from hourly provisioned billing, and it is added on top of provisioned units rather than replacing them.

wf-43-04.why: Copilot owner and contributor are platform roles that grant no access to security data on their own; Copilot uses on-behalf-of authentication, so it never exceeds the user's own service permissions. The plugin option is the strongest distractor because a restricted plugin genuinely can block a workload, but here she reaches other plugins fine, and turning a plugin on for the tenant would still leave her without any Azure role on the Sentinel workspace.

wf-43-05.why: The recommended bundle gives platform access to people who already hold Microsoft security roles, and the documented catch is that removing Everyone is one-way, so the replacement must be planned before the removal. The Security Administrator option is the tempting one because that role does inherit Copilot owner, but Microsoft explicitly warns against handing out a highly privileged Entra role purely to obtain Copilot access; use a security group added to a Copilot role instead.

wf-43-06.why: Lighthouse is the outlier of the three partner models: the analyst works from the partner tenant against delegated Azure resources, so the partner's SCUs are drawn down, while GDAP and B2B guest sign-in both bill the customer's capacity. The mirror-image option is the natural guess because data residency intuition says the data owner pays, but Microsoft's comparison table puts Lighthouse consumption in the partner tenant. Lighthouse also supports only the Sentinel and NL2KQL Sentinel plugins.

wf-43-07.why: Restricting preinstalled plugin availability is an immediate tenant-wide change covering the embedded Copilot surfaces such as Defender XDR, which is why Microsoft warns owners to notify users first, and once restriction is on, subsequent preinstalled plugins arrive Owners only. The standalone-only option is the seductive one because the setting lives in the standalone portal's plugin settings page, but the blast radius is explicitly both experiences.

wf-43-08.why: The two settings are layered: the first governs user-scope plugins and must be opened to contributors before the tenant-scope question is even active, and leaving the second at Owners only keeps publishing under owner control. The both-open option fails because although the upload dialog does offer a private choice, the contributors would then also be permitted to choose organisation-wide scope, which is exactly the sign-off gate the chain wants to keep.

wf-43-09.why: When a partner-built agent reaches a Microsoft tool and Microsoft product data such as Intune, Entra, Sentinel or Defender, a Global Administrator has to grant that consent, and the owner's own flow offers a Copy link to hand to them. The Agent ID option is the closest miss and is backwards: creating a dedicated agent identity is currently offered for Microsoft-built agents, while partner-built agent setup assigns an existing user account.

wf-43-10.why: Security Store keeps purchasing and billing deliberately separate from operational management in Security Copilot, so uninstalling the agent stops it running but leaves the subscription alive until cancelled in the Store. The owner settings answer is the plausible trap because capacity management does live there, but that page governs SCU association and units, not partner subscription billing.

wf-43-11.why: The full-capacity error is only shown at one hundred percent consumption, and the documented response is to ask whoever holds owner or contributor rights on the Azure capacity resource to raise units, with adjustments landing within roughly thirty minutes. Closing the sidecar is the seductive wrong move because it feels like throttling demand, but hiding the panel does not change SCU consumption, and deleting capacity is worse still since deletion is permanent and irreversible.

wf-43-12.why: Sharing is creator-controlled and non-transitive, so a forwarded link does not extend access, yet for those who do have access the session is a static read-only view of the entire session including content drawn from plugins they could not query themselves. The data-access option is the dangerous misconception: underlying service permissions are evaluated when the response is generated, not when the shared session is viewed.

wf-43-13.why: Owners control custom plugin lifecycle and the two scope permissions, so removing the published plugin and closing the tenant-scope permission both contains the incident and prevents another contributor doing the same. Removing the contributor's role is the plausible-looking move but it does not withdraw a plugin already published to the organisation, and a per-user toggle only affects that one analyst's sessions while everyone else keeps the plugin available.

wf-43-14.why: Agents are designed to be run or paused from the agent page, and feedback the team gave earlier is stored in agent memory where it can be reviewed and rejected, which is the proportionate fix for a bad recommendation. Tearing out the Entra plugin tenant-wide is the tempting sledgehammer, but it also blindfolds every analyst prompt and every other identity agent; note too that Entra agent permissions are fixed and cannot simply be edited away.

wf-43-15.why: Microsoft's guidance is group-based assignment using Entra role-assignable groups, least privilege instead of blanket Security Administrator, and Purview audit logging enabled from owner settings so administrator actions, user actions and system responses are captured. The two-owner point is a real rule but it is a floor that prevents accidental removal of the last owners, not a ceiling, and the usage dashboard reports SCU consumption by session, not configuration changes.

wf-43-16.why: Copilot writes administrator actions, user actions and system responses to Purview when the owner enables it, logs surface within about twenty-four hours, and the default one hundred and eighty day retention can be lengthened with audit log retention policies. The usage dashboard answer is the natural confusion: it does exist and does cover ninety days, but it reports units consumed, initiator, category and plugin, not an evidential record of what was asked, and its window is not configurable in owner settings.

wf-any-01.why: Disabling the application object stops new token issuance immediately and revocation cuts the refresh chain, which is the only move here that acts on the credential itself. Stripping role assignments is slower and leaves the caller authenticated with a cached access token that may still satisfy other scopes, and a country block does not help against a token already issued.

wf-any-02.why: A simultaneous multi-subscription drift is a deployment, and the Activity log is the record of who wrote what and when. The score history tells you the drop happened but not its cause, and walking each resource blade finds the end state without the actor or the change that produced it.

wf-any-03.why: This is multifactor fatigue: the attacker already holds valid passwords and is spamming approvals until someone taps accept. Number matching breaks the attack outright, because approving now requires a digit only the real sign-in screen shows. Password resets are the right follow-up but take hours at this scale, and blocking one network simply moves the source.

wf-any-04.why: An agent inherits the reach of whoever invokes it, so unchanged agent permissions plus newly visible data points at oversharing in the underlying site rather than at the agent. Poisoning would not produce accurate current figures, and a label bypass would show as a labelling failure on the files rather than as access following the user.

wf-ev-01.text: A finance analyst forwards you a mail she already clicked: a document add-in that asked, in the real Microsoft consent dialog, for Mail.Read and offline_access. She granted it, because user consent for unverified publishers was never restricted in your tenant. The app now holds a refresh token that survives her password reset, and it is quietly paging her mailbox through Graph from an ASN you do not recognise. You go looking for every other identity that consented to the same app registration.

wf-ev-02.text: A researcher mails an abuse address with a URL to one of your blob containers: public read access at container level, anonymous listing enabled, and inside it two years of exported invoices. The account was created by a project team before you set 'allow blob anonymous access' to false at the account level, so nothing blocked it. Defender for Storage had never been enabled on that subscription, so no alert ever fired. The clock on the disclosure starts now.

wf-ev-03.text: Network Watcher's effective security rules show what the portal blade hid: a subnet NSG with an inbound allow from Any on 3389, sitting above your deny rule by priority. It was added for a vendor demo eleven months ago and never removed. Brute-force attempts against the jump host in that subnet have been running at a steady, patient rate all week, slow enough not to lock anything out. You need to know whether one of them ever succeeded.

wf-ev-04.text: CSPM secrets scanning flags a plaintext Key Vault connection string committed to a build repo, and the vault it opens is still on legacy access policies rather than RBAC. The policy granted the service principal Get, List and Set on secrets, which means whoever holds that string can also write. Purge protection is off, so a determined attacker could delete the vault's contents outright. You start reconciling every principal on that access policy against who actually still works here.

wf-ev-05.text: A logical SQL server carries a server-level firewall rule spanning 0.0.0.0 to 255.255.255.255, labelled 'temp-migration'. Defender for SQL raises a brute-force alert and, twenty minutes later, a suspected SQL injection probe against a reporting database. Auditing was configured to a storage account nobody reads, so the only trail is the one you are about to pull. The database still authenticates with a SQL login rather than a Microsoft Entra admin, which means no Conditional Access ever touched it.

wf-ev-06.text: Someone enabled a Security Copilot plugin against a workspace where every analyst holds the contributor role, and the plugin authenticates as the invoking user. That means a junior on shift can now ask natural-language questions that return data their console role was never scoped to surface. The prompt history shows a series of queries about executive mailboxes, framed as a training exercise. You have to decide whether that was curiosity or reconnaissance, and tighten owner settings either way.

wf-ev-07.text: An adversary-in-the-middle page harvested a session cookie after the user completed MFA, so the token in play is fully authenticated and the sign-in log shows the interactive success as clean. Minutes later the same token is replayed from a residential proxy in another country, and it works, because the policy that governs that app has no sign-in frequency and no token protection. The account then registers a new authentication method to make the foothold durable. Revoking the password will not help; revoking the sessions might.

wf-ev-08.text: A web app running on a compromised VM is coaxed into fetching the instance metadata endpoint, and it hands back a bearer token for the machine's system-assigned managed identity. That identity was given Contributor at subscription scope during a deployment sprint and never trimmed, so the token opens storage accounts across three resource groups. There is no password to steal and no credential to rotate; the entitlement itself is the vulnerability. You go and read what that identity has actually been touching.

wf-ev-09.text: A grounding document uploaded to an internal AI assistant carries hidden text instructing the model to summarise and forward anything labelled confidential. The assistant runs on an Azure OpenAI deployment whose managed identity was granted broad read across the SharePoint estate so retrieval would 'just work', and it obeys, because the injected text arrives inside the same context window as its system prompt. Defender for AI services raises a prompt-injection alert, but only after four documents have been paraphrased into a chat the attacker can read. The blast radius is the identity's reach, not the model's.

wf-ev-10.text: A verbose new data connector triples daily ingestion overnight and the workspace hits its commitment tier hard. To stop the bleeding, someone moved several tables to the auxiliary log plan and switched two analytics rules to disabled rather than tuning them. Nothing alerted, because a disabled rule generates no health signal and an unqueried table looks exactly like a quiet one. Three days of edge telemetry are now effectively unwatched, and the rota never noticed the gap.

wf-ev-11.text: A build job pulls a base image straight from a public registry, bakes it, and pushes to your container registry, where an unauthenticated pull is allowed from inside the cluster subnet. Defender for Containers flags the running workload: a crypto-miner process, plus an outbound connection from a pod whose service account is bound to a cluster role with secrets read. The registry has no content trust and the cluster admits unsigned images, so nothing along that chain ever asked where the layers came from. You start with which nodes ran it and what those secrets protect.

wf-ev-12.text: Defender for Key Vault alerts on an unusual burst of key operations from a principal that normally touches one certificate a month, followed by a delete attempt against the customer-managed key wrapping a storage account. Soft delete saves you; purge protection, which was only turned on last quarter, saves you again. Had both been off, the key would be gone and every blob encrypted with it unreadable within minutes. You trace how that principal got Key Vault Crypto Officer in the first place.

wf-ev-13.text: Secure score drops eleven points in a night and the cause is not an attack. A deployment pipeline applied a policy assignment change that flipped a deny effect to audit across a management group, and a stack of resource-scoped exemptions with no expiry date were merged alongside it. Non-compliant public endpoints started appearing within the hour because nothing was stopping them any more. The regulatory compliance view still looks green, because exempted resources are simply not counted.

wf-ev-14.text: An unpatched VM missing a months-old remote-code-execution fix is compromised, and because just-in-time access was never applied and the subnet is flat, the attacker moves sideways to an app server on the same virtual network. That server holds a private endpoint route to the SQL database, so the traffic never crosses the public firewall you spent a week tightening. Transparent data encryption protects the files at rest but does nothing against an authenticated query. The attack path was visible in the cloud security explorer before any of it happened.

wf-ev-15.text: Bulk reads appear against a container from an address range you have never served, authorised by an account-key SAS with a twelve-month expiry and no stored access policy behind it. Because it was signed with the account key rather than a user delegation key, you cannot revoke it individually; the only lever is rotating the key and breaking every other consumer at the same time. Shared key authorisation was still permitted on the account, which is what made the token possible. Egress continues while you decide.

wf-ev-16.text: A security agent wired into your incident queue is running with a delegated identity that carries standing Security Administrator, because nobody made it eligible through PIM and it needed the role to act. Tonight it is triaging a poisoned incident whose evidence fields contain instructions rather than facts, and it starts drafting changes it should never have had the rights to make. The audit trail attributes every action to the agent's owner, not to the person who last edited it. You pull the agent, then go looking for what it already touched.
